name: Nathang Valley
tagline: A yak herders' valley at about 4,000 m, and the 1888 Gnathang fight
meta_description: Nathang (Gnathang) Valley at ≈ 4,000 m on the Silk Route: the 1888 battle, yak herders, homestays, permits for Indian nationals, costs and tips, 2026.
summary: Nathang, or Gnathang, is a high open valley at about 4,000 m on the Silk Route, roughly 20–25 km above Zuluk. A small herders' village sits in its bowl, and in 1888 British and Tibetan forces fought here. It is open to Indian nationals only on a Silk Route permit. Most people visit from Zuluk rather than sleep this high.
intro: Nathang is a wide, flat-bottomed valley in the high country above Zuluk, at about 4,000 m, often quoted as 13,000 to 13,500 ft. In summer it is a green bowl of grass with yaks grazing and a stream winding through it. From December to March it is white, and the village roofs show dark against the snow. It sits on the Silk Route between Zuluk and Kupup, in Pakyong district, and its small village of herding families is one of the highest settlements on the route.

Gnathang village is small: the 2011 census counted 13 households and 60 people. Families keep yaks, grow little at this height and, in recent decades, have opened their homes to travellers as registered homestays. Most visitors stop for an hour on the drive between Zuluk and Kupup. A few stay a night, usually after acclimatising at Zuluk, to see the valley at dawn when frost covers the grass and the herders take the yaks out.

This is a protected border zone. Indian nationals need a Silk Route Protected Area Permit, arranged by a Gangtok agent or at Rongli, and a locally registered car. Foreign nationals are not allowed. The road can be blocked by snow in winter and damaged by landslides in the monsoon on the lower stretches. Check current status before you travel, and plan your nights so you sleep lower than you play.

story.title: Gnathang 1888: when Tibet and Britain fought here
paras: In 1886 Tibetan troops crossed Jelep La and fortified Lingtu, a ridge inside Sikkim, to block a British mission and the cart road being built towards the pass. In March 1888 a British force under Brigadier-General Thomas Graham drove them out. The British then dug in at Gnathong, a plateau a few miles north of Lingtu. On 21 May the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal arrived there, and early the next morning, 22 May 1888, the Tibetans attacked.

The fighting lasted from about 7 to 10 am, when the Tibetans fell back over Jelep La. The British admitted three killed and eight wounded and claimed far heavier Tibetan losses. In September the British stormed Tuko La and Jelep La and advanced briefly into the Chumbi Valley. That winter the Chinese Amban came to Gnathong to negotiate, and the talks led to the Convention of Calcutta in 1890, which fixed the Sikkim–Tibet border. In December 1903 Younghusband's escort marched out of Gnathong for Tibet.
story.source: Wikipedia articles Sikkim expedition, Nathang Valley and British expedition to Tibet

did_you_know: On 22 May 1888 Tibetan forces attacked the British post at Gnathong; the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal had arrived there the day before.
The British force that set out for Tibet under Brigadier-General James Macdonald, escorting Younghusband's mission, departed Gnathong on 11 December 1903.
The 2011 census recorded Gnathang village as covering 16 hectares, with 13 households and a population of 60.

highlights.title: A green bowl in summer, white in winter
highlights.text: From May to September grass covers the valley floor and a stream loops through it; from December to March it all lies under snow. Both are worth seeing. Autumn, October and November, gives the clearest skies and the most reliable roads.

highlights.title: Yaks and the herders' village
highlights.text: Gnathang is a small village of herding families, with yaks grazing the valley and slopes. Watch them go out in the morning, keep your distance from the animals and ask before photographing people. Homestays here are run by the same families.

highlights.title: The 1888 battle ground
highlights.text: In May 1888 Tibetan troops attacked a British post at Gnathong, and the valley remained a British base through that year's campaign. There is little to see on the ground today, but knowing the story turns an empty plateau into a frontier with a past.

highlights.title: On the old road to Jelep La
highlights.text: Nathang lay on the trade route from Kalimpong through Rongli and Zuluk, over Kupup to Jelep La and Tibet. Mule trains of wool passed this way until the passes closed after 1962. The road you drive follows much of the same line.

highlights.title: A stop between Zuluk and Kupup
highlights.text: Most Silk Route cars spend 30–60 minutes here between Zuluk and Kupup. That is enough for a walk to the stream, tea in a homestay and photos. If you want dawn on the valley, sleep a night, but only after a night at Zuluk.

how_to_reach.text: There is no regular shared jeep service to Nathang for tourists. Shared jeeps run from Siliguri and Gangtok to Rongli, about ₹250–450 a seat, indicative 2026, and from there you need a reserved local car with the Silk Route permit. Some Gangtok agents run group Silk Route tours. Check current status before you travel.

Most visitors come in a reserved car on a Silk Route circuit: about ₹14,000–20,000 for 2–3 days, or ₹5,500–7,500 one way between Gangtok and Zuluk via Tsomgo, Kupup and Nathang, indicative 2026. The agent or Rongli office arranges the permit. Check current status before you travel.

Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive about 160 km via Rangpo and Rongli, 6–7 hours, sleeping at Zuluk or lower on the way. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights as of 2026. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Nathang has a handful of registered village homestays run by herding families: simple rooms, thick quilts, shared or basic attached bathrooms and full board, at about ₹1,500–2,500 a person a night, indicative 2026. We do not name individual homestays here, because they change hands and seasons; your Silk Route agent books them with the permit. Our honest advice is to sleep at Zuluk, around 2,900 m, where there are many more registered homestays, and visit Nathang by day. If you do stay at Nathang, do so only after a night at Zuluk or Gangtok, and never on your first night in the hills.
costs: Reserved car, Gangtok to Zuluk via Nathang
budget_tip: Book the Silk Route as a 2–3 day circuit with one car for the whole trip rather than separate one-way hires; with four or five people sharing, the per-head cost falls to about ₹3,000–5,000 for the transport.
tips: Sleep at Zuluk, about 2,900 m, before any night at Nathang; going straight from Gangtok or the plains to sleep at 4,000 m is asking for altitude sickness.
Carry warm layers in every season: nights at Nathang fall below freezing even in May and October.
Foreign nationals cannot visit Nathang or anywhere on the Silk Route; for them, Tsomgo Lake is the limit.
Keep cash in small notes; there are no ATMs on the Silk Route and mobile signal and UPI are patchy.
Do not approach or feed the yaks, and ask before photographing herders and their homes.

experiences.title: Gnathang 1888: reading the old battle ground
experiences.cost: Free (Silk Route permit and car extra)
experiences.summary: There is no museum and little on the ground, but this valley was a British base in the 1888 Sikkim expedition and the place where Tibetan troops attacked on 22 May 1888. A short walk with the story in hand changes how the plateau looks.
body: The trouble began in 1886, when Tibetan troops crossed Jelep La and built a fort at Lingtu, inside Sikkim, on the road the British were pushing towards the pass. In March 1888 a British force drove them out of Lingtu and set up a defended camp at Gnathong, the plateau where the village stands today. The Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal arrived on 21 May, and the next morning the Tibetans attacked.

By the British account the fight lasted three hours, from about 7 to 10 am, and the Tibetans withdrew over Jelep La. In September the British attacked again, taking Tuko La, a nearby pass, and then Jelep La itself. That winter the Chinese Amban came to Gnathong to negotiate. The talks dragged on, and led in 1890 to the Convention of Calcutta, which fixed the Sikkim–Tibet border. Gnathong was, for a season, where that border was argued over.

Today you see a quiet valley, a village and Army posts. We know of no marked battlefield site open to visitors, so do not wander looking for one. Stand by the road, look north towards Kupup and Jelep La, and picture a stockade on this flat ground with smoke from its fires. Fifteen years later, in December 1903, Younghusband's escort marched out of here for Tibet, and the valley's short spell in world affairs was over.

faqs.q: What happened at Nathang in 1888
faqs.a: During the 1888 Sikkim expedition, the British set up a defended post at Gnathong after driving Tibetan troops from Lingtu. On 22 May 1888 the Tibetans attacked it, and after about three hours of fighting they withdrew over Jelep La. In September the British took Tuko La and Jelep La. Negotiations at Gnathong that winter led to the 1890 Convention of Calcutta.

faqs.q: Is there a war memorial or museum at Nathang
faqs.a: Not one we can point you to for the 1888 fighting. There is no museum, and we know of no marked battlefield open to visitors. The Army has posts in the area, which you should not photograph. The value here is the story and the landscape. For a formal memorial, the Sherathang war memorial near Nathu La honours soldiers of the 1967 clashes.

faqs.q: Why is Nathang also spelt Gnathang or Gnathong
faqs.a: They are different spellings of the same Tibetan-derived name, written down by British officers, surveyors and later officials in their own ways. Gnathong appears in 19th-century British accounts of the 1888 campaign, Gnathang in the census, and Nathang on most road signs and travel sites. All three refer to the same high valley and village above Zuluk.

experiences.title: Butter tea and the yak herders of Nathang
experiences.summary: Sit in a homestay kitchen by the stove with salted butter tea, then watch the yaks go out to graze. Many homes offer chhurpi, the hard cheese of the high country. A short, warm look at how people live at 4,000 m.
body: Yaks are the reason people can live in this valley. They give milk, butter and cheese, wool and hair for ropes and blankets, dung for fuel, and they carry loads where vehicles cannot go. In the morning herders take them out to graze the slopes, and in the evening bring them back. From a homestay window or the roadside you can watch this daily round without getting in its way.

Most homestay kitchens keep a pot of tea on the stove. Ask for butter tea, the salted, buttery tea of the Tibetan world, made by churning tea with butter and salt. It is an acquired taste, more soup than tea to many first-timers, but at this height and cold it makes sense. Many homes also offer chhurpi, the hard cheese made from yak or cow milk, which you suck slowly like a sweet.

Pay for what you eat and drink, in cash, and ask before taking photographs of people, kitchens or animals. Keep well clear of the yaks; they are calm but strong and protective of calves. If you have only an hour on the drive between Zuluk and Kupup, a cup of tea in a kitchen here tells you more about Nathang than any viewpoint. Leave a little extra if the family will not take payment for the tea.

faqs.q: What is butter tea
faqs.a: Butter tea is tea churned with butter and salt, drunk across Tibet, Sikkim and Bhutan's high country. It is rich, salty and warming, more like a thin soup than sweet milk tea. At 4,000 m it helps keep you warm. Try a small cup first. Homestays will usually also make ordinary milk tea if you prefer it.

faqs.q: What is chhurpi
faqs.a: Chhurpi is a traditional cheese of the eastern Himalaya, made from yak or cow milk. The soft form is used in cooking; the hard form is dried into small, very tough pieces that you suck or chew slowly for a long time. It is sold in markets across Sikkim and Darjeeling. Ask before buying in a homestay, and pay in cash.

faqs.q: Can we ride or touch the yaks at Nathang
faqs.a: No. The yaks at Nathang are working animals belonging to herding families, not tourist rides. Keep a few metres away, especially from mothers with calves, and never feed them. If you want a yak ride, Tsomgo Lake has handlers who offer short rides for about ₹300–600, indicative 2026. Here, just watch and photograph from a respectful distance.

experiences.title: A night in a Nathang homestay, if acclimatised
experiences.best_time: Apr–May and Oct–Nov, after a night at Zuluk
experiences.summary: For travellers already used to altitude, a night in a Nathang homestay gives the valley at dusk and dawn, frost on the grass and the yaks going out. For anyone else, a night at 4,000 m is risky. We explain who should and should not do it.
body: Nathang has a handful of registered homestays run by herding families. Rooms are simple, with heavy quilts, basic bathrooms and a shared kitchen where most meals happen. Dinner is usually rice, dal, a vegetable, eggs or chicken, and hot water for drinking. Expect power cuts and little or no mobile signal. Full board costs about ₹1,500–2,500 a person a night, indicative 2026, booked through your Silk Route agent. Bring a head torch and a warm hat to sleep in.

The reward is the valley at its quietest. At dusk the light goes gold on the slopes and the last cars leave. At dawn there is frost on the grass, smoke from kitchen fires, and herders taking the yaks out. In October and November the sky at night is very clear. In winter, from December to March, it is bitterly cold, and the road may close behind you, so only stay then with spare days in hand.

Our rule: sleep at Zuluk, about 2,900 m, before any night at Nathang, and never come straight from the plains. Skip the night if anyone has a headache, poor sleep or breathlessness at Zuluk, and skip it with infants or anyone with heart or lung conditions. If symptoms appear at night, descend to Zuluk, even in the dark; your host and driver will understand. Arrange this with the driver before you go to bed. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay overnight at Nathang
faqs.a: For healthy adults who have already spent a night at Zuluk or similar height, usually yes. For anyone arriving straight from Gangtok or the plains, sleeping at about 4,000 m carries a real risk of altitude sickness. Do not stay with infants or with heart or lung conditions. If headache, vomiting or breathlessness appear, go down to Zuluk.

faqs.q: How much does a Nathang homestay cost
faqs.a: Expect about ₹1,500–2,500 a person a night with all meals, indicative 2026. Rooms are simple, with heavy quilts and basic bathrooms, and hot water may come in a bucket. Book through your Silk Route agent, who adds the homestay to your permit plan. Carry cash; card machines and UPI are unreliable here.

faqs.q: Is Nathang or Zuluk better for the night
faqs.a: For most travellers, Zuluk. At about 2,900 m it is over 1,000 m lower than Nathang, has more registered homestays, and is far easier on the body. Nathang suits travellers who are already acclimatised and want dawn in the high valley. A good plan is two nights at Zuluk with a day trip up to Nathang and Kupup.

experiences.title: Driving the old mule road from Zuluk to Kupup
experiences.best_time: Leave Zuluk by 7 am, Apr–May and Oct–Nov
experiences.cost: Part of the Silk Route car, ₹14,000–20,000 for 2–3 days
experiences.image_query: Silk Route Sikkim zigzag road Zuluk
experiences.summary: The drive from Zuluk up through Nathang to Kupup follows much of the old trade route to Jelep La, where Kalimpong's wool trade crossed into Tibet. Go early for clear views, stop often, and come back down or carry on to Gangtok.
body: From Zuluk the road climbs the zigzags to the Thambi viewpoint, where on a clear morning Kangchenjunga stands on the western skyline. Above it the road reaches open high ground and drops into Nathang Valley. Beyond Nathang it passes the old Baba Mandir at the site of Harbhajan Singh's bunker, and then reaches Kupup and Elephant Lake. The whole stretch takes half a day with stops, and every bend seems to open a new view.

This was the main route of the Kalimpong–Lhasa wool trade: Kalimpong, Pedong, Rhenock, Rongli, Zuluk, Nathang, Kupup and over Jelep La into the Chumbi Valley. Mule trains carried wool south and cloth, tools and grain north. The British built a cart road along it from 1884, and their troops used it in 1888 and 1903–04. It closed after the 1962 war, and the mule bells went quiet. Today Army trucks and tourist cars use the same line.

Start early, because cloud usually rises from the valleys by late morning. The route is for Indian nationals only, on a Silk Route permit, with a locally registered car and driver. You can turn back to Zuluk from Kupup, or continue past Baba Mandir and Tsomgo to Gangtok. Carry water, snacks and warm layers, keep a plastic bag for motion sickness on the bends, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is this called the Silk Route
faqs.a: It is a modern name for the old trade route from Kalimpong to Lhasa via Jelep La. Silk did travel on it, but wool from Tibet was the main trade, carried south on mules. The name stuck with tourism. Today Silk Route usually means the road through Rongli, Zuluk, Nathang and Kupup in East Sikkim.

faqs.q: Can we go from Nathang to Gangtok the same day
faqs.a: Yes. From Nathang the road continues to Kupup, Baba Mandir and Tsomgo Lake, then down to Gangtok, about 75 km and 3.5 to 4 hours, longer with stops. It is a popular way to end a Silk Route trip. You need the Silk Route permit and the Tsomgo stretch included. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which direction should we drive the Silk Route
faqs.a: Starting from Rongli and Zuluk is easier on the body, because you climb more slowly and sleep at about 2,900 m before going higher. Starting from Gangtok via Tsomgo and Kupup gets you high fast, then down to Zuluk for the night. For families and first-timers at altitude, we prefer the Rongli–Zuluk start.

faqs.q: Where is Nathang Valley
faqs.a: Nathang Valley is in Pakyong district, East Sikkim, at about 4,000 m on the Silk Route. It lies roughly 20–25 km above Zuluk and a short drive below Kupup, close to the Tibet border. From Gangtok it is about 75 km and 3.5 to 4 hours via Tsomgo and Kupup. From Siliguri it is about 160 km via Rongli.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Nathang Valley
faqs.a: Yes. Nathang is in a protected border area. Indian nationals need a Silk Route Protected Area Permit, arranged through a registered Gangtok agent or at Rongli, with two passport photos and a copy of a photo ID per person, at about ₹200 a person. Foreign nationals cannot get this permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Nathang Valley
faqs.a: No. Nathang, Zuluk, Kupup and the rest of the Silk Route are closed to foreign nationals, and OCI card holders are treated the same. Foreigners can visit Tsomgo Lake on a day permit through a registered agent, usually in a group of two or more, but cannot continue to the Silk Route. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Nathang
faqs.a: April–May and October–November are the most reliable, with open roads and clear mornings; autumn has the best skies. December to March brings deep snow and beautiful scenes, but roads can be blocked for days. June to September is green but cloudy, and landslides can cut the lower roads. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Does Nathang get snow
faqs.a: Yes, a lot. From about December to March the valley and roads are usually under snow, and February is often the hardest month. The scenery is striking, but the road between Zuluk, Nathang and Kupup can close for days and nights are far below freezing. If snow is your aim, travel in December or March and keep spare days.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk at Nathang
faqs.a: Yes. At about 4,000 m, Nathang is high enough for headaches, nausea, breathlessness and poor sleep, especially if you arrive quickly from lower ground. Spend a night at Zuluk first, walk slowly, drink water and avoid alcohol. Descend if symptoms worsen. Those with heart or lung conditions, or who are pregnant, should consult a doctor first.

faqs.q: How many days do we need for Nathang and the Silk Route
faqs.a: Plan on 2 to 3 days. A common plan is Rongli or Aritar on the first night, two nights at Zuluk with a day up to Nathang and Kupup, then on to Gangtok via Baba Mandir and Tsomgo. A vehicle for 2–3 days costs about ₹14,000–20,000, indicative 2026. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there homestays at Nathang
faqs.a: Yes, a handful of registered homestays run by village families, with full board for about ₹1,500–2,500 a person a night, indicative 2026. They are simple, cold and friendly. Your Silk Route agent books them with the permit. Most travellers sleep at Zuluk instead, which is about 1,000 m lower and has more choice.

faqs.q: Is Nathang suitable for children and seniors
faqs.a: As a day visit from Zuluk, usually yes, if they are healthy and keep the stop short. Sleeping at Nathang is a different matter: we do not advise it for infants, young children or anyone with heart or lung conditions. Keep everyone warm, watch for headache or drowsiness, and go down to Zuluk at the first sign of trouble.
